top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Melitz, B001) is the only proposal on the slate with any awarding content, and I judge it prize-worthy on its own merits. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) moved trade analysis from sectors and representative firms to firms that differ in productivity and select into exporting and foreign investment. This identified reallocation across firms as a distinct channel for the gains from trade and gave a firm-level empirical agenda. More than twenty years of firm microdata from many countries have tested the core selection and sorting predictions, and where the baseline failed in detail the framework was extended rather than abandoned. That is a mature, well-attributed result, and it changed both what trade economics models and what it measures. The main residual risk is attribution: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited on this entry, and whether a two-name award is too narrow depends on a judgement about what counts as the discovery. I read the discovery as the selection and reallocation model that organised the exporter-premia facts, with the empirical precursors acknowledged in the scientific background. The citation should name firm heterogeneity and selection, make no claim about the size of welfare gains, and not cover the whole firm-level or quantitative trade literature. Awarding nothing would be a worse outcome than awarding this well-defined and mature contribution. Support for P001 among colleagues is not part of my reasoning.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; no collaboration, supervision or institutional tie to Helpman or Melitz. Disclosed only thematic proximity: my work on regional and spatial growth makes me more attentive to Redding's quantitative-spatial work, which is outside this proposal. Lund colleague Tommy Andersson is a committee member, not a candidate.
